prompt.context: Our client owns a designer shoe-store that makes high-end made-to-measure shoes for customers. The high-quality product has gained popularity rapidly and the client wants to ramp up production. However, the highly-skilled labor that the client employs is hard to come by.
prompt.question: Our client wants us to help them figure out how to increase output without adversely affecting quality. How would you approach this?

clarifying_info.q: Are there additional skilled shoemakers available in the market?
clarifying_info.a: No, there are no additional skilled shoemakers available in the market.

clarifying_info.q: What does the shoe-making process look like?
clarifying_info.a: The shoe-making process has 3 stages: cutting, stitching, and finishing.

clarifying_info.q: How many workers are there and how long does it take to make a pair?
clarifying_info.a: There are currently 15 workers, each of whom takes an average of 12 hours to produce one pair of shoes.

clarifying_info.q: How is the work currently divided among the shoemakers?
clarifying_info.a: Each shoemaker currently performs all three steps of the process.

clarifying_info.q: Do different shoemakers have different skill levels for each step?
clarifying_info.a: Yes — different shoemakers have different skill-sets. [Provide Exhibit 1 at this point.]

clarifying_info.q: Can we change the process so that shoemakers perform only specific tasks?
Is there any technology available to boost output?
clarifying_info.a: No, there is currently no technology we can use to boost output.

exhibits.title: Employee Survey — Hours per Activity by Group
exhibits.shows: A table showing how many hours each of three employee groups (5 employees each, 15 total) takes to complete each of the three production steps: cutting, stitching, and finishing.

data.note: These numbers are from a survey conducted among the 15 employees at the client's workshop. The groups reflect the fact that different employees specialize in particular aspects of the process.

framework: Understand the current production process end-to-end (steps, time, resources)
Assess current labor utilization — how are 15 skilled workers allocated across tasks?
Identify misalignment between individual skill-sets and the tasks each worker performs
Evaluate whether specialization (task-based division of labor) is operationally feasible
Quantify the output improvement from specialization and calculate new weekly profit
Assess implementation risks and next steps

questions.prompt: Given Exhibit 1, how should the process be restructured to maximize output, and what is the resulting time per pair of shoes?
questions.guidance: The candidate should recognize that each group has a different hour-per-task profile. The optimal assignment is to allocate the task to the group fastest at it: Group 1 handles Cutting (3 hrs), Group 3 handles Stitching (3 hrs), Group 2 handles Finishing (3 hrs). Each pair therefore passes through one group per stage, totaling 3+3+3 = 9 hours per pair — down from 12 hours. The key insight is specialization reduces per-pair time by 25%.

math.setup: Assign each stage to the group with the lowest hours for that stage. Cutting: Group 1 = 3 hrs (best). Stitching: Group 3 = 3 hrs (best). Finishing: Group 2 = 3 hrs (best). New total time per pair = 3 + 3 + 3 = 9 hours.
steps: Identify minimum hours per stage across groups: Cutting min = 3 (G1), Stitching min = 3 (G3), Finishing min = 3 (G2)
Reduction from 12 hrs to 9 hrs = 25% improvement
math.answer: 9 hours per pair under the specialized system

questions.prompt: What is the maximum weekly output and weekly profit under the new specialized system?
questions.guidance: The candidate should work through a structured calculation: hours available per employee per week → pairs per employee → total pairs. Then apply price and cost assumptions to arrive at weekly profit. All numbers are given in the math info; the bottleneck insight (9 hrs/pair) from Q1 is the critical input.

math.setup: Given: 9 hrs/pair, employees work 9 hrs/day × 5 days = 45 hrs/week, 15 employees total. Price $300/pair; materials $40/pair; shipping $10/pair; wages $15/hr; fixed costs $1,000/week.
steps: Hours per week per employee = 9 hrs/day × 5 days = 45 hrs
Pairs per employee per week = 45 hrs ÷ 9 hrs/pair = 5 pairs
Total weekly output = 5 pairs × 15 employees = 75 pairs
Materials and delivery cost per pair = $40 + $10 = $50

brainstorming.prompt: What risks or implementation challenges might arise from switching to a specialized task-based production system?

categories.name: Employee / Change Management
ideas: Workers accustomed to completing full pairs may resist the change
Loss of craft identity or job satisfaction for skilled artisans
Need for retraining on focused tasks even if workers already have the skill

categories.name: Operational / Layout
ideas: Workshop layout may need to be reconfigured to support task-based flow
Risk of bottlenecks if one group's capacity doesn't match the others
Work-in-progress inventory between stages must be managed carefully

categories.name: One-Time Transition Costs
ideas: Temporary productivity dip during the transition period
Potential quality issues while workers adapt to new roles

categories.name: Quality & Brand
ideas: End-to-end ownership by one craftsperson may have ensured quality accountability — need new QA checkpoints
High-end brand perception may rely on the 'one artisan per shoe' narrative

recommendation: Change the production process from one where each shoemaker performs all three steps to a specialized system where each of the three groups focuses exclusively on its strongest task (Group 1 on cutting, Group 2 on finishing, Group 3 on stitching).

This reduces average production time per pair from 12 hours to 9 hours — a 25% improvement — enabling a 25% increase in output (from ~60 to 75 pairs per week) using the same 15 workers, without hiring additional labor or compromising quality.
risks: Employee resistance to changing an entrenched process
One-time costs for potential workshop layout changes
Temporary productivity loss or quality variability during the transition
Loss of individual craftsperson accountability for end-to-end quality
next_steps: Pilot the specialized system with a small subset of workers to validate the 9-hour target and identify implementation issues before full rollout.
Monitor quality metrics closely during the transition and establish stage-level quality checkpoints.
Implement the change in a phased manner to minimize disruption and allow workers to adapt gradually.
Evaluate whether additional process improvements (e.g., workflow sequencing, workstation design) can further reduce per-pair time beyond 9 hours.
